title: Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox with Statistical Models
claim: Different estimators give valid but increasingly precise uncertainty estimates, with model-based estimation giving the narrowest valid intervals for the same accuracy.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, each with CI-width dots above accuracy bars
description: Two side-by-side panels, each with two vertically stacked plots that share an x-axis of four LLMs (Llama 3.1 40B, Phi 4, O4 Mini Medium, Gemini 2.5 Pro). The shared legend at the top has a pink square for simple average (1 trial), a blue triangle for regression-free (8 trials) and an orange circle for GLMM (8 trials). In the left panel (a), benchmark accuracy, the top plot shows CI width as dots. Pink dots sit high, near 0.10 to 0.14, and blue dots sit low, near 0.03. Below them, pink and blue bars show similar accuracy, with black error bars that are much wider for pink. In the right panel (b), generalized accuracy, the top plot has pink dots highest, blue in the middle and orange lowest. Below, grouped bars in three colors have matching heights, and the error bars shrink from pink to blue to orange. The eye goes first to the colored dot ordering.
caption: Accuracy estimates (GPQA Diamond). Lower plots show estimated accuracy of each LLM with 95% confidence intervals.
abstract: Benchmarks are widely used to evaluate and compare the performance of artificial intelligence systems. However, some approaches to computing benchmark metrics produce invalid uncertainty estimates or make unrecognized assumptions about the evaluation setting. We leverage statistical modeling to make two contributions to the practice of AI benchmarking. First, we formally distinguish measurements of benchmark accuracy from generalized accuracy (performance on all potential test items similar to those included in the benchmark). Then, in a simulated setting and with large-scale evaluation of 22 API-access frontier large language models on 3 popular benchmarks, we show how analysis via generalized linear mixed model can produce correct estimates of generalized accuracy while more efficiently quantifying uncertainty compared to existing regression-free approaches. We also show how this approach can equip evaluators with important context on evaluation results, including variance decomposition and item difficulty estimates that illuminate important aspects of LLM performance and benchmark construction.
